newsitem.title: Indonesia: East Timor's Bishop Belo returns to Dili.
newsitem.headline: East Timor's Bishop Belo returns to Dili.

text.p: East Timorese Bishop Carlos Belo returned home to an orderly welcome on Saturday after mass demonstrations in Dili through the week against Indonesian criticism of the Nobel peace prize winner.

East Timor's deputy police chief Colonel Atok Rismanto said about 5,000 people met him at Dili's Komoro airport around noon off a scheduled flight from Jakarta, and followed him to the city's cathedral where he was due to say an afternoon Mass.
"They had banners that read 'Viva Belo', but there were no problems. They were orderly and everything went smoothly," Rismanto told Reuters by telephone from Dili.
He said earlier about 500 people had been driving around the small coastal city since early morning in convoys of privately-owned trucks, cars and motorcycles in anticipation of the bishop's return.
"He's disembarked from the plane and passed my office (in the city centre) on the way to the cathedral," Rismanto said following Belo's return to the territory's capital.

"The bishop will soon give a mass. They (the crowd) have followed him to the cathedral. Maybe we won't have any problems because the bishop is a community leader who is very influential. If he says don't (do something), they won't."

Mass demonstrations led initially by students at the University of East Timor in central Dili started last Tuesday in protest against criticism of Belo by Indonesian officials and in the media and protest demonstrations in Jakarta.

The bishop, jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel peace prize with self-exiled East Timorese-born independence activist Jose Ramos Horta, was reported to have said in an interview with a German news magazine that Indonesian troops treated East Timorese like "dogs".
Belo, who spent the week in Jakarta attending an annual meeting of Indonesian Roman Catholic bishops, has refused to comment until he sees a full transcript of the interview.

The only incident reported by police during the demonstrations was the stoning of the local legislature on Wednesday in which Rismanto said a few windows were broken and a car was damaged. There have been no arrests during the week.
Religious affairs officials in Jakarta have called for calm and said the reported interview was not a religious affair.
Religion has become a touchy issue in the largely Moslem country of nearly 200 million people following the burning of 25 Christian churches in eastern Java last month.

The attacks by an angry mob started during a trial of a local Moslem in a Situbondo court for blasphemy against Islam. Religious scholars said the church burnings resulted at least in part from local social and economic frustrations.
Belo himself is regarded as possibly the most influential civilian in mainly-Catholic East Timor.
Indonesian troops occupied the former Portuguese colony in December 1975 and it was declared the country's 27th province the following July.
